chase_cards.name: Cleffa
chase_cards.why: This row is a chase because it is a small card with a surprisingly large footprint: Johto's baby-Pokemon idea, CoroCoro's monthly insert machine, Sugimori's official species language, and the Eek draw-card memory all converge.

key_artists.name: Ken Sugimori
key_artists.why: Sugimori matters here because baby Pokemon needed immediate visual legibility. Cleffa's star-shape and soft official pose make the new Johto category readable before any collector starts arguing about variants.

claims.text: The local catalog models the CoroCoro Comic February 2000 issue insert as a one-row unnumbered promotional source group containing Cleffa at source index 156.
Bulbapedia's Cleffa page says the Japanese print was available as an unnumbered promotional card on an insert in the February 2000 issue of CoroCoro Comic, released January 15, 2000.
PokeBoon and Pokumon both frame this Cleffa as a 2000 CoroCoro magazine promo, with Pokumon tagging it as Colorless, Unnumbered, Ken Sugimori, Non-holo, Japanese, and Glossy.
The official Pokemon site lists Pokemon Gold and Silver as released in Japan on November 21, 1999, placing this January 15, 2000 Cleffa insert in the first months of the Johto launch moment.
A collector reference to CoroCoro insert culture describes CoroCoro Comic as a monthly Shogakukan manga magazine and notes that it is known for including Pokemon promotional cards.
Bulbapedia credits the Cleffa illustration to Ken Sugimori.
PokeBoon and Pokumon also credit this CoroCoro Cleffa promo to Ken Sugimori.
Bulbapedia identifies Cleffa as a Colorless-type Baby Pokemon card, HP 30, with the attack Eek drawing 2 cards.
Bulbapedia says the Japanese print features the Gold, Silver, to a New World... symbol and that the bottom border reads CoroCoro Comic February issue bonus card.
This Cleffa matters because it joins three separate kinds of early-2000 Pokemon assembly: new Johto species education, baby-Pokemon game mechanics, and CoroCoro's monthly promo-distribution rhythm.

Confirm the card is Cleffa / ピィ as an unnumbered Japanese promotional card, not merely any Cleffa card.
Preserve Ken Sugimori as illustrator where scan or citation allows.
Check for Colorless Baby Pokemon frame/text and the Eek / ピッピッ draw-card attack where image quality allows.

narrative.human_title: Cleffa: the baby star in CoroCoro's Johto machine
narrative.why_it_matters: Cleffa looks tiny until you let the assembly come into focus. Gold and Silver had just opened Johto, baby Pokemon were teaching players that evolution could have a prehistory, and CoroCoro put that idea directly into a glossy insert. The card is sweet, but also mechanical: Baby Pokemon protection, Eek, two cards drawn, a little star-shaped creature making the new era playable. This is why the catalog cannot only rank trophies. Sometimes the important card is the one that taught a generation how the world had expanded.

The art matters because Sugimori's simple star-shaped Cleffa makes a new baby-stage concept immediately readable as cute, small, and mechanically different from the older Clefairy line.

The card should be checked as the Japanese CoroCoro February 2000 unnumbered promo with Gold/Silver symbol and CoroCoro February issue bonus-card border text, not merely as Cleffa or Wizards Promo 31.

narrative.human_title: Cleffa: a tiny rulebook for Johto
narrative.why_it_matters: Cleffa is sweet enough to disappear into the binder if you only sort by spectacle. But this little CoroCoro insert is doing serious assembly work. It carries Sugimori's new Johto baby-language, teaches the Baby Pokemon defensive flip, offers Eek as a tiny draw engine, and wears the Gold/Silver symbol like a flag planted in the new era. It is the kind of card that makes the catalog feel alive: small, glossy, monthly, and absolutely part of how Pokemon taught people what Johto was.
